content Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure INTRODUCTION Municipalities have Constitutional responsibility for providing sustainable and viable water services to the communities within their areas of jurisdiction
The purpose of these guidelines is to assist municipalities undertake the development of water and sanitation infrastructure with focus on the design aspects of development
Further guidelines are in the process of being developed for Water Services Development Plans social aspects and operation and maintenance of water services projects

Purpose of guidelines It is important to ote that these guidelines uf ARE MERELY INTENDED TO GIVE GUIDANCE TO MUNICIPAL OFFICIALS PLANNERS AND DESIGNERS uf Are ot intended to replace professional expertise and engineering judgement uf Provide overarching guidance and cannot be used as replacement for specifications uf Must be used together with recognised standards codes and acts such as those of the South African Bureau of Standards SANS Codes the Water Services Act the National Water Act and the Occupational Health and Safety Act These guidelines are made available through two media uf CD has been distributed which contains this document as well as umber of useful folders
The contents of the folders are listed at the end of this document uf downloadable version of the document is also accessible from the web page of the Department of Water Affairs and Forestry

The DWAF web page also contains the same folders that are included on the CD Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure Definitions of minimum orms and standards The aim of Water Services projects funded out of government grants is primarily to provide basic level of water services
Section of the Strategic Frame work for Water Services provides the minimum technical orms and standards for water services
The Strategic Framework is included in the Legislation and Policy Folder

The following definitions and minimum standards are given in the Strategic Framework Basic water supply facility is The infrastructure ecessary to supply litres of potable water per person per day supplied within metres of household and with minimum flow of litres per minute in the case of communal water points or litres of potable water supplied per formal connection per month in the case of yard or house connections

Basic water supply service is The provision of basic water supply facility the sustainable operation of the facility available for at least days per year and ot interrupted for more than consecutive hours per incident and the communication of good water use hygiene and related practices

Basic sanitation facility is The infrastructure ecessary to provide sanitation facility whic is safe reliable private protected from the weather and ventilated keeps smells to the minimum is easy to keep clean minimises the risk of the spread of sanitation related diseases by facilitating the appropriate control of disease carrying flies d pests and enables safe and appropriate treatment and or removal of human waste and wastewater in an environmentally sound manner

Basic sanitation service is The provision of basic sanitation facility which is easily accessible to household the sustainable operation of the facility including the safe removal of human waste and wastewater from the premises where this is appropriate and ecessary and the communication of good sanitation hygiene and related practices

Potable water quality is Water supplied by water services providers intended to be used for drinking or domestic purposes potable water must be of quality consistent with SANS Specifications for Drinking Water as may be amended from time to time
Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure Metering and flow control All unrestricted water connections must be metered or controlled to basic level

Where appropriate water services providers should consider the benefits of offering households controlled flow connections for example yard tanks that can provide basic supply of water cost effectively
Where pre payment meters are installed these must take into account the free basic water services policy and allow for access to basic amount of water at zero tariff
Eradication of bucket toilets The bucket system is an unsuitable and inappropriate level of service
All water services authorities must identify and implement programmes for the eradication of all bucket systems by

Project development life cycle A typical project development life cycle consists of the following phases Establishment of institutional arrangements The designated municipality is the water services authority and is responsible for water services provision
The water services authority either contracts with water services provider or fulfils that function itself

Planning phase The municipality uf prepares Water Services Development Plan WSDP as part of its Integrated Development Plan IDP for the area of jurisdiction of the Water Services Authority WSA uf undertakes Feasibility Studies for each water or sanitation project identified in the WSDP DWAF integrates all WSDPs into National Reference Framework
Design phase The municipality procures the design consultant who designs the works and prepares the tender documentation or the municipality does it in house
Tender stage Advertising site inspection adjudication of tenders received and award of contract

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure Construction phase Execution of the works in accordance with the tender documentation under supervision Operations and maintenance The Water Services Provider operates and maintains the works with or without the assistance of contractors and collects the revenue
The Water Services Authority WSA monitors the Water Services Provider WSP and manages he contract that it has with the WSP
The WSA undertakes an annual water services audit and reports to DWAF who performs the function of Regulator

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure LEGISLATION AND POLI CY A umber of important statutes and policy documents govern the development and operation of community water supply schemes

Legislation affects all phases of development and for example stipulates requirements for taking water from the resource for the planning of water services how to determine institutional arrangements and th requirements for financial and other reporting

The most important legislation and policy documents governing the development and operation of water services are uf Constitution of the Republic of South Africa Act of uf Water Services Act Act of uf National Water Act Act of uf Municipal Systems Act Act of uf Municipal Structures Act Act of uf Public Finance Management Act Act of uf Local Government Municipal Finance Management ct Act of uf Division of Revenue Act Enacted Annually uf Strategic Framework for Water Services September uf White Paper on Sanitation September uf Regulations under of the Water Services Act uf Regulations under of the Water Ser vices Act uf Regulations under of the Water Services Act uf Model Water Services Bylaws
Section of the Water Services Act uf Guidelines For Human Settlements Planning and Design Red Book
The full text of hese documents with the exception of the Red Book are included in the Legislation and Policy folder of the guidelines CD
Most of these documents must be read with Acrobat Reader which is available on the Web Specific sections of these documents will al so be highlighted in the different sections of the Guidelines

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure INSTITUTIONAL ARRANG EMENTS Introduction The following institutions are responsible for the supply of water and sanitation services uf The Water Services Authority uf The Water Services Provide Sometimes Water Board or bulk water provider and uf The Department of Water Affairs and Forestry as regulator
For example DPLG manages the Municipal Infrastructure Grant and the Equit able Share and the Department of Health has an important function regarding health and hygiene and sanitation
A Water Services Authority WSA is the municipality that has been designated responsibility for ensuring access to water services
The WSA is oth the owner of the works and is the elected representative of the customers
A water services provider WSP is the person or organization that actually provides water services to consumers or to another water services institution
The WSA can either appoint WSP for example another municipality water board or private contractor or can fulfil the function itself

Deciding on and contracting with water services provider The WSA should follow the procedure set out in of the Municipal System Act when deciding whether it should fulfil the WSP function itself or whether it should contract with separate WSP
model Terms of Reference for Assessment has been developed by the Municipal Infrastructure Unit MIU which is associated with BSA
This model Terms of Reference is included in the Institutional Folder
S of the Water Services Act sets out requirements that must be complied with when WSA contracts with WSP
The Minister has promulgated regulations under of the Water Ser vices Act which sets out the minimum requirements with which contract between WSA and WSP must comply

Even if the WSA fulfils the WSP function itself it should account separately for water services it should Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure uf keep separate financial accounts of how much was spent on or invested in water services during each financial year uf the revenue it received from the sale of water services uf funds received from National Government and ther sources that were allocated to water services etc
Bylaws and other requirements S of the Water Services Act requires that WSAs must make bylaws which contain conditions for water services
Model Bylaws that comply with the requirements of of the Water Services Act are included in the Legislative and Policy Folder

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure PLANNING Introduction Water and sanitation projects are essentially planned at three levels uf At the ation al level the Department of Water Affairs and Forestry DWAF maintains ational reference framework uf At municipal level each Water Services Authority WSA compiles and regularly updates Water Services Development Plan WSDP and uf At project level each WSA undertakes feasibility study for each project and compiles technical report

This hierarchy of plans are discussed below National reference plan The Department of Water Affairs and Forestry is required to comment on the Water Services Deve lopment Plans WSDP of each WSA and to ensure that all current and projected activities are compatible with the ational strategies

To enable common framework for assessing WSDPs National Reference Plan is being developed which will capture the ess ence of each WSDP in one common structure that relates water services planning to the National Water Resource Strategy Catchment Management Strategies together with water allocations and licensing Provincial Strategies and IDPs

The reference framewor will cover the following topics uf General Locality map and Demographics uf Physical Socio Economic Development uf Water resource availability allocation and licensing uf Service Level Development uf Water Resource Development uf Water Conservation Demand Man agement uf Water Services Infrastructure uf Water Services Authority Institutional Arrangement uf Customer Services uf Financial Profile and uf Project Development
Municipalities will eed to cross reference their plans to the National Reference Framework in order to integrate their own planning with other developments being undertaken in surrounding areas

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure Water services development plan Sections to of the Water Services Act requires Water Services Authority to prepare Water Services Development Plan
These sections describe how to develop and adopt WSDP and sets out the contents of the WSDP
The Water Services Act is included in the Legislation and Policy Folder
Whilst the WSDP is legal requirement the real value of preparing WSD lies in the development of plan whereby the key municipal water services targets are set for five year period
The WSDP forms subset of and must be aligned to the municipality Integrated Development Plan IDP
The Department of Water Affair and Forestry has prepared set of Guidelines for preparing WSDP
These Guidelines provide basic information about the WSDP as well as specific information on how to prepare the WSDP

Feasibility studies and technical reports The aim of Water Services projects funded by municipalities out of government grants is primarily to provide basic level of services to the poorer residents of the municipality
Previously project level business plans were compiled by municipalities for purposes of project approval and allocation of funds by ational government
Under the Municipal Infrastructure Grant MIG it is o longer ecessary for municipalities to submit business plans to National Governm ent for approval

However municipalities are still required to plan for projects feasibility studies and to submit Water Services Project Technical Report to the appropriate DWAF Office for recommendation before releasing funds for water services proje cts
It is recommended that the same approach be followed for all Water Services projects

It is requirement that the establishment of potable ground water sources should be executed under the controlled supervision of qualified and suitably experienced hydrogeologists geologists geophysicists and hydrogeological technicians
The hydrogeological services required during project implementation are as follows uf Assessment of existing groundwater sources

This may require the test pumping of existing boreholes rehabilitation or re drilling of boreholes chemical analysis of water samples from existing boreholes and an examination of documentation relating to the reliability and sustained discharge rate of existing boreholes

In areas with marginal water quality testing of ewly drilled boreholes or equipped existing boreholes should ot commence prior to availabilit of chemical analysis results of TDS NO and uf Borehole siting

The hydrogeologist is responsible for ensuring that appropriate scientifically based methods are used to identify suitable drilling targets sites in accordance with hydrogeological condi tions for exploration drilling

In order to ensure safe working conditions and to limit the risk of pollution entering the groundwater abstraction facility borehole sites are also affected by the existence of manmade structures such as roads pipelines emetries sewage plants overhead powerlines buildings etc
The hydrogeologist is responsible to ensure that boreholes are drilled designed and constructed to the required stand ards by controlled and on site supervision of drilling rigs
One supervisor is to supervise at least two drilling rigs up to maximum of three drilling rigs
uf Supervision of borehole test pumping and administration of testing contracts

The hydrogeologis is responsible to ensure that the required and appropriate calibration multi rate draw down constant discharge and related recovery tests are conducted to the required standards by on site and controlled supervision of testing contractors
Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure uf Borehole yield recommendations
Motorized borehole pumps are generally warranted only in instances where discharge rate in excess of can be maintained for continuous pumping period of eight hours or more per day
Borehole yields must always be determined on the basis of hour per day pumping
technical report documenting all data and information is required on completion of investigations
The project hydrogeologist is required to ensure that data requirements from the hydrogeologist and ontractors are documented on appropriate data recording forms and submitted to DWAF
This comprises the removal of drilling fines from the aquifer pores removal of drilling foam mud and establishing reverse filter around the bore hole aquifer interface
Duration of development can vary from couple of hours formation stabilizer hard rock formations to several days unconsolidated fine sandy aquifers
Boreholes must also be disinfected or sterilized of any bacteria and particu larly coliform bacteria intruded into the borehole during drilling operations
The borehole is protected from foreign material by means of lockable cap fitted to the borehole collar
The borehole should be marked with pole meters to the orth of the borehole of approximately high with umber plate showing the borehole identification umber
The pump testing contractor is required to test ewly drilled boreholes which have ot yet be en equipped and existing boreholes which may or may ot already be equipped with pumping installations
The type of borehole test methods required include Slug Test Calibration Discharge Test Stepped Discharge Test Constant Discharge Test Recovery Test uf Monitoring the resource
The geohydrologist must develop monitoring system for at least one full hydrological year to evaluate the resource response to the safe yield abstraction rate
After this period the monitoring program should be re assessed and pla ned according to prevailing climatic conditions
Borehole pumps The pump specified must ot be capable of exceeding the safe yield of the borehole when utilized over hour period
Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure The rest and pumping water levels in borehole may vary considerab ly during drought and above average rainfall sequences
Choice of type of borehole pumping plant must take this into account

The selection of the particular pumping unit must also take into account the following factors uf The static head between the lowes drawdown level anticipated in the borehole and the delivery point at the borehole top
uf The friction generated in this length of rising main given due attention to the presence of any operating rods within the rising main
uf The static and friction heads fr om the top of the borehole to the top water level of the delivery point
uf The ability of the pumping plant to commence operation under the full static head conditions of the pump unit
uf The ability of the pump to start operation with the riser pipe empty

uf The level at which the pumping unit has to be placed in the borehole must be as specified by the hydrogeologist or based on reliable information known to the engineer should hydrogeologist ot be available
Borehole pumps can be powered by means of line upply electricity solar power or diesel power

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure DAMS AND WEIRS Dams In some cases dams will be required to store surface runoff and to provide the bulk wate supply source
The size of the dam is dependent on the water demand the required assurance of delivery the hydrological characteristics of the river and the characteristics of the dam basin
The type of dam to be constructed will amongst others de pend on site configuration topography foundation conditions and the availability of suitable construction materials
Weirs Where dam is used for bulk water storage and the water is released down the river it may be ecessary to construct weir at the point of abstraction
The purpose of the weir is usually to provide limited balancing storage for the bulk releases from the dam

Weirs can also be constructed to store limited amounts of runoff or even by allowing the basin to be filled with alluv ial material to create reservoir within the alluvial sand from which water can be abstracted
In the case of weirs siltation is far greater problem than in the case of large or medium sized dams
The outlet works and abstraction points of weirs eed to be kept free of silt
Weirs generally being of limited height and capacity will also be overtopped by large floods
They will therefore eed to be constructed of concrete or other on erodable material
A site for weir where both the riverb ed and the abutments consist of good quality rock is an ideal situation
More usually the weir is founded on rock in the river section and one or both of the abutments will comprise of soft river bank materials
In this case special measures are required prevent outflanking of the structure by large floods
Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure Approved professional engineer Dams are site specific
The Dam Safety Regulations may require that an Approved Professional Engineer APE assume responsibility for the design depending on the si te capacity and hazard potential of the dam
The classification of proposed dam is done by the Dam Safety Office of DWAF upon submission of an application listing the pertinent data
Dams can be categorized into the following categories uf Category uf Category II and uf Category III
The design of weirs should also be undertaken or supervised by competent engineers who are conversant with the particular problems associated with these structures

Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure Outlet pipe systems Dual system outlets should be provided in order to ensure continuous outlet from the water sources during repair or maintenance of the main outlet

At the most upstream point of the outlet pipe system an emergency closure by means of an underwater wall type spindle driven sluice gates operated by manual actuators may be employed only if the size of the outlet is in excess of mm diameter
Intake entrance The most upstream exit from the dam reservoir should consist of bellmouth
Maintenance of bel lmouths is practically impossible due to leakage through the isolating gate seals if gates are employed and limited working space downstream of such gates
Intake bellmouths and adjacent pipework should thus be fabricated from stainless steel up to the ownstream isolating valve
Should the pipework downstream of the isolating valve be built into concrete or buried in earth this pipework should also be fabricated from stainless steel
Accessible pipework in any outlet system pipes which are expose and are removable may be fabricated from mild steel and corrosion protected
Reducers and pipework directly adjacent to valves should be of fabricated steel
The coupling of built in steel or HDPE pipework hould be SABS or BSS flanges only and should be rated according to the hydrostatic pressure of the outlet works
Friction grip couplings are unacceptable in other cases as well except where construction joints occur
Air supply pipes should be fitted to the outlet bellmouth top and extended to above the high flood level of the dam
The air pipe should be at least th of the diameter of the outlet pipe
Control valves for outlet works Isolating valves Pipe outlets should be provided with valve downstream of the pipe entrance to facilitate maintenance of the control valves and downstream pipework
Pipe outlets up to mm in diameter should be provided with open port resilient seal valve RSV type gate valves
Guidelines for the development of water and sanitation infrastructure Rising and on rising spindles are acceptable

Pipe outlets exceeding mm diameter should be fitted with butterfly valves double flanged or wafer type having horizontal spindles only so as ot to be affected by silt build up on the bottom of the pipe
For small dams and weirs manual actuation can be specified for all isolating valves
Manual operation is to be provided as far as possible due to the low cost and lower mainten ance

Larger valves may be fitted with manually operated gearboxes to limit operating forces on the hand wheels or levers to kN Isolating valves should all be situated in fully accessible boxed out chambers having suitable drainage facilities
Valv es situated in chambers less than deep should be provided with extension spindles which are operable from the deck of the chamber
Valves in chambers more than deep should be accessible via vertically mounted access ladders
All isolating val ves should be removable by means of either approved flange adapters or in line pipe couplings situated directly downstream of such valves

Supports should be provided under pipework at either side of dismantling couplings excepting in cases where such co uplings are converted to thrust absorbing couplings by means of studs and thrust collars
Control valves Control valves are to be situated at the end of outlet works pipelines to facilitate controlled flow outlet from the dam
resilient seal valve RSV type gate valves are acceptable control valves for small dams and shall as far as possible be manually operated
In cases of free discharge into rivers adequate protection must be given to the environment in the immediate vicinity of the valve to preve t erosion
Control valves eedle type Only in extreme instances where low head loss is important should in line eedle valves be used for controlled water outlet from the dam or weir
Since eedle valves are mounted in the pipeline their energy diss ipating qualities are ot as effective as sleeve valves

It is thus advisable to either provide the pipe exit downstream of the valve with flared disperser which is to be shaped to cause hydraulic jump or alternatively the exit should disperse into stilling chamber

Under water wall mounted sluice gates These gates are generally spindle driven units which are secured in sealing frame where sufficient movement is provided upwards for the gate to clear the inlet fully open and for the downward stroke to seal off the opening completely

The headstock which is to be mounted on the concrete deck of the outlet works may be of mild steel fabrication galvanised

Rising spindle designs are essential since experience has proven that submerged drive nuts used on on rising sp indle designs renders the gate inoperable due to algae and other debri suspended in the water which enters the drive ut thread

uf The pump performance curves are then plotted on the same graph

uf An ideal pump election will result in each Pump Duty Point falling at or very near to the pump Best Efficiency Point BEP
uf When only one pump in multi pump arrangement is operating the intercept with the system curve will be at point of reduced head and increased flow with regard to the chosen Pump Duty Point

IW CDS Revision Misconnection Allowance Urban Creep Urban Creep Urban Creep is the loss of permeable area within urban areas creating increased run off from ew impermeable areas which contributes to reduced sewer capacity increased potential flooding and occurrence of pollution incidents due to overflows from SWOs or hydraulic overloading of WWTPs
Urban creep principally impacts combined sewers storm water sewers and the downstream atural drainage systems
It should be oted that urban creep tends to increase over time and may be egligible early on in the asset life

In areas served by combined sewer systems the growth in impermeable area or urban creep causes increases in surface water run off being conveyed to the combined sewers and storm water sewers thus reducing capacity increasing frequency of storm water overflow spills and increasing the risk of se wer flooding
Allowance for urban creep shall be in accordance with Irish Water Guidance Note on the Application of Urban Creep Allowances and Misconnections for Future Scenarios in Wastewater Modelling

Misconnection Allowance Where there are separate wastewater and storm water sewer etworks the rainfall response in wastewater etworks due to storm water inflow is principally caused by misconnections of storm water drains sewers to the separate wastewater sewer storm water drains being connected to the wastewater drain sewer either unintentionally or intentionally as convenient method of dealing with storm water runoff on premises
However rainfall response can also be due to direct inflow through defective covers or indirectly via ainfall induced infiltration

Misconnections can occur at the outset of ew development due to poor construction practice either within the building around the curtilage of the building or in the public road due to the connection of the service pipe or gully to the incorrect public sewer system storm water source being connected to wastewater sewer system
The misconnection conveys storm surface water run off from the impermeable area via the storm drain or sewer to the wastewater sewer
Rainfa ll response in wastewater sewers can be many multiples of orders of magnitude greater than wastewater flow
IW CDS Revision This increased inflow response can utilise significant capacity can significantly reduce the design horizon and can cause pollution incidents and ewer flooding

Most public wastewater sewers have misconnections and over time some wastewater sewers will exhibit flow response of partially separate sewers wastewater sewer which also carries some storm water flow

While removing the misconnectio is preferred finding and addressing the problem is ot always feasible even with extensive intrusive sewer surveys CCTV surveys flow rainfall surveys which will employ substantial resources and result in significant expenditure outlay
It is consi dered therefore far more cost effective to minimise its occurrence in the first place
To preserve capacity in public wastewater sewers an increased flow allowance for misconnections should be provided for in the design of public sewers
This would also apply to ew wastewater sewerage system of certain scale in ew developments that will be connected to public sewerage systems

General The suitability of plumbing materials in low cost housing units has to be viewed from the perspe ctive of pricing its water saving capabilities durability and the risk of it being stolen for its scrap value
An important item although ot material related is the location of water meters in low cost housing schemes
Often where the meter is locat ed on lot accessibility for reading purposes is compromised when occupants later erect high fences for security reasons
The best position for the meter is outside the property in an undercover location on the footway or vertically mounted against the welling very effective for low coat housing
Material It should also be borne in mind that all materials must comply with the relevant SA NS JASWIC Joint Acceptance Scheme for Water Installation Components standards

However provision has been made in the by law for Council to use pipes fittings and other plumbing components which are ot on the Jaswic list should this be required in order to evaluate the suitability of ew materials for spec ific applications
Pipes and piping systems for underground use in the supply of potable water
An important part in the installation of water pipes in underground locations is the condition of the soil in which the pipe is to be laid
If it is con taminated with chemical substances this could affect the durability of the pipe
It would also determine the material of which the pipe is manufactured
Copper Copper pipe is historically the preferred material in the Cape Town region
For underground use only class is allowed because of its thicker wall
Class pipe is however much more expensive than the other clas
Copper pipe should ot be laid in soil that contains ash salt and chemicals such as ammonia and magnesite
These substances will cause pitting of the wall of the pipe
Polypropylene polycop This type of plastic pipe is very popular for underground use
The Wat er Services Hillstar depot has been using it for the installation of ew water connections ranging in size from to mm since approximately and it has proven to be very reliable
The brass Conex fittings could prove to be expensive especial ly in the larger sizes
It should ot be laid in soil that is contaminated with petrol oil and umber of other chemicals
These chemicals permeate through the wall of the pipe resulting in bad taste and smell in the drinking water
In such cases the ly solution is to replace the pipe with class copper since the smell and taste lingers and cannot be eliminated from the plastic pipe
This condition affects all pipes and fittings manufactured from plastic polymers and is therefore ot only restricte to polycop piping

For this reason in the case of plans approval for service station we call for copper pipe to be used in both above ground and underground applications in the forecourt area where invariably spills of oil petrol will take place
It is imperative that only SA NS approved class polycop pipe is used
It has been found that the lighter class pipe is ot so durable
HDPE high density polyethylene This plastic pipe has also gained popularity for underground use
Personal experience has shown that with age underground leaks tend to be problematic
This is found to be the case when we have to process rebate claims for underground defects on private properties
It has also been fo und that moles have special affinity for these pipes and many an underground leak is due to hole having been gnawed into the pipe
Other types of plastic pipes There is ho st of other plastic pipes and pipe systems for potable water installation on the market
Of late these include composite pipes which combine layers of plastic and Aluminium to form tube
The problems with many of these systems are that special tools are required to facilitate its installation and that the fittings are ot always readily available
Galvanised mild steel pipes It should be oted that in line with our Water services by law galvani sed mild steel pipes and fittings are ot allowed to convey water supplied from the Municipality mains
This is because our water is only chemically stabilised for copper systems
It is also soft and therefore aggressive in ature and re acts with other metallic pipes such as galvanised steel and Aluminium
In the case of pipes serious encrustation forms on the inside of the pipes thereby diminishing its bore
This eventually causes poor supply pressures and restricted flows from erminal fittings
According to the Red Book pipes may have to be above ground due adverse conditions such as rock
When considering laying pipes above ground the following factors eed to be taken into account uf Provision should be made for expansion the effects of thermal changes must be considered
The supports should be designed to carry the load of the pipe as well as the water it conveys
Suffici ent support should be included in order to prevent sagging of the pipeline
The pipe should be strapped to the support leaving room for movement
uf Adequate thrust blocks should be designed to cater for hydraulic forces at bends
uf Adequate anchoring should provided especially in steep slopes and directional and elevation changes
uf Adequate protection should be provided to cope with external abrasion
Material used for piping system above ground All the previously mentioned pipes except for galvanised mild steel pipes can be used in above ground installations
Class is an extremely hard thin walled pipe which should ot be formed into labour bends
Because of its hardness compression fittings should also ot be used
Any change of direction in the piping system should be achieved by the use of copcal capillary soldered fittings
full range of tee pieces and bends of various angles is provided for this purpose
Class pipe has thicker wall than class and is in turn thinner walled than lass
Both classes and can be formed into labour bends which reduces the need for fitting saves time during installation and gives improved flow
Although copper pipe systems are durabl and very popular with plumbers in above ground applications it is prone to theft

This can be problematic in low cost housing where we have experienced in certain instances that the occupants of the house have in fact removed brass and copper from the plumbing system to be sold as scrap
In its effort to avoid this type of behavior the maintenance section of Housing Department is investigating the use of an all plastic threaded type of piping system
Copper systems are also more expensive than co mparable plastic pipe installations
Some plastic pipes have conditions imposed when used in hot water installations
None of the plastic pipes in use at present is approved for use in fire and combined fire domestic installations in above ground locations due to its combustibility
Should pipe rupture during fire it would result in severe pressure loss rendering the fire fighting system ineffective
For this reason only copper and black steel piping ca be used in above ground locations in fire fighting installations
Taps and Stopcocks It is oted with concern that all the less expensive chrome plated taps for kitchen sinks and wash hand basins have spouts that cannot accommodate water savin aerator
This device is only catered for on the more expensive models
An in line flow controller supplying less than litres per minute installed in the supply line to the tap should solve this problem
This would also conform to the by law requir ement that basin tap should ot discharge more than litres per minute
Ball valves ballostops should be used in place of stopcocks since they are less expensive and also have better flow characteristics
Service Guidelines Standards for Water and Sanitation Department CCT In the case of outside garden taps pla stic tap would be most suitable since it doesn represent much in terms of scrap value

Council can permit it to be installed without JASWIC approval as per the pr ovision of the by law but experience has shown that in ormal use as garden tap it is ot very durable
Water closet cisterns There are various models of cisterns on the market
One of the most suitable for low cost housing is the litre Shires duranite unit
It is available for both low level and high level applications
It is extremely rugged in construction and is fitted with dual flush siphon valve
This ty pe of flushing mechanism does ot cause water to trickle leak into the pan when the system is ot in use

This problem is ormally experienced with the type of flushing valve that employs flapper rubber to seal off the water at the bottom of the cister This leakage can be tremendous source of wastage since it ormally carries on around the clock until it is repaired
This type of wastage would ormally go undetected in low cost housing units
Another one of this cistern positive features is plastic float valve with an Aluminium arm
Brass float valve arms are ormally removed and sold for its scrap value
The diaphragm fitted to the siphon ormally lasts for more than years before replacement is required
With this type of cistern an exte rnal overflow pipe is installed

Any overflow of water from it due to defective float valve would be readily discernible whilst this will ot be the case with flapper rubber type valve which has an internal overflow as an integral part
If there were sufficient height for its installation copper tank combination gravity feed hot water cylinder would be the best option for low cost housing
This type of cylinder has float valve similar to the one installed in he cistern and therefore its maintenance is minimal
However because it is an open to the atmosphere system heat loss is experienced
This open system places little strain on the inner tank and consequently this type of cylinder should last indefinitely
Where the plumbing design cannot accommodate combination hot water cylinder a pressurised system will have to be installed
Service Guidelines Standards for Water and Sanitation Department CCT The and kPa copper tank cylinders are the ext best options
Some and kPa units have galvanised steel inner tanks and these require sacrificial anode to protect it against the corrosive effects of the aggressive soft water being supplied by Council
This anode has to be inspected regularly and eplaced when this becomes ecessary
The lower delivery pressure of the and kPa copper tank cylinders also contributes to saving of water since this equates to lower flow rates at terminal fittings
Both types of pressurised hot water cylinders require pressure reducing valve pressure relief valve sometimes the two are combined temperature and pressure safety valve and vacuum breakers
This increases the installation and maintenance costs when compared with the combination hot water cylinder
Due to pressure variations being exerted on the inner tank of pressurised hot water cylinder these units ormally do ot las as long as combination hot water cylinder
Galvanised tank cylinders have been known to rupture after only years in service
Brazing can usually repair the copper tank cylinder whilst defective galvanised steel tank cylinder will have to be discar ded if the tank has ruptured

Service Guidelines Standards for Water and Sanitation Department CCT CHAPTER KOSOVO VACUUM SEWER SYSTEM

SYSTEM DESCRIPTION Unlike conventional gravity systems which depend solely on gravity flows vacuum sewer systems make use of combination gravity and differential air pressure as the driving force that propels sewage through the sewer etwork
Vacuum sewer systems consist of three key components collective chambers vacuum sewers and the vacuum station

Figure Major components of vacuum sewer systems As constructed in Kosovo toilets cubicles at each sanitation block are drained through mm diameter uPVC pipes to an adjacent vacuum valve pit containing the collection chamber sensor unit and an interfac valve

Once predetermined volume of sewage has accumulated in the collection chamber the pneumatically activated sensor unit prompts the opening of the interface valve which links the collection chamber to the vacuum sewer etwork
When the interface alve opens the sewage followed by short burst of air is sucked into the vacuum sewers

Each input of energy occurring as the each interface valve along the etwork opens further propels the sewage along the vacuum sewer etwork consisting of to diameter pipes until it reaches the vacuum station where it accumulates in vacuum vessels

Vacuum pipe work Collective chambers Vacuum station Service Guidelines Standards for Water and Sanitation Department CCT The vacuum station houses the vacuum pumps which generate and maintain the negative pressure in the vacuum vessels and throughout the vacuum sewer etwork
The sewage that accumulates in the vacuum vessels is evacuated by sewage pumps and is conveyed to sewer outfall where it joins an existing gravity sewer
Figu re The Saw Tooth method used for the vacuum sewer lines
Figure Collective chamber Service Guidelines Standards for Water and Sanitation Department CCT

Advantages Vacuum sewerage has the advantage of enabling the use of conventional flush toilets without the eed for deep trenches large diameter sewers umerous access manholes and the eed to always travel in straight lines as is customary with waterborne sewerage

The use of reduced diameter pipelines and shallow trenches in Kosovo reduced the disruption caused retrofitting sewer etwork in the informal settlement by minimizing the umber of shacks that had to be moved to allow for construction

Due to the flat gradients sandy soils and high water tables in the area the installation of conventional ravity sewer system would have used mm diameter pipes installed at depths of up to and incorporating three lift stations
As result of the high transport velocities within the vacuum sewers the risk of sewer blockages is reduced
Major leaks in the system are also immediately evident as suction is lost in the system making vacuum sewerage particularly useful in environmentally sensitive area

Constraints A dis advantage of vacuum sewerage is that the system operation can be disrupted by a disruption in the power supply to the vacuum pump station and carelessness when using the toilets by flushing down foreign objects Cutlery stones sticks etc
result ing in the vacuum pumps ot being able to generate the egative pressure required for the system to operate
In addition to this the malfunctioning of an interface valve or sensor unit would result in the toilet units draining to the specific collection chamber being rendered unusable
